evaluation.positioning_hook: A rule-bound young union member risks his future to pursue a cross-state romance, then gets pulled into the organization’s propaganda machine when his feelings become politically useful.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is immediately legible and commercially sticky: a controlled romance inside a coercive social system, with a clear forbidden-love engine and a sinister institutional backdrop. It’s narrower than a four-quadrant thriller because the world is specific and the ending is more satirical than explosive, but the hook is strong enough to sell on concept alone.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early in the outing system, the score-based dating ritual, and the cross-local restriction that turns a romance into a bureaucratic violation. By the time Lewis kisses Emma and gets flagged, the premise is fully understood and the escalation is clean.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Lewis has a clear internal contradiction: he’s trained to be compliant, but the script keeps finding the pressure point where his sincerity leaks through. Emma is a strong counterforce, and Chance Hunter is a vivid antagonist, though the supporting cast is more functional than deeply individualized.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s most distinctive move is turning romance into a monitored civic process, then revealing how easily intimacy can be converted into state messaging. The final propaganda montage is a bold tonal and conceptual pivot that gives the material a sharper satirical edge than a standard dystopian love story.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story escalates cleanly from ceremony to outing to escalation to executive review to the road trip and interview trap. The middle section is procedural by design, which keeps the engine clear but also means the script’s momentum is more controlled than relentless.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea feels fresh and immediately ownable: a state-managed pairing system where emotional authenticity becomes both a liability and a commodity. It’s familiar in its dystopian DNA, but the specific mechanics of the Union app, scoring, and cross-local review make it feel newly engineered.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world has rules, signage, rituals, and bureaucratic language that all reinforce the same social order: approved restaurants, outing scores, behavioral review, executive consultation, and propaganda imagery. The Union feels like a functioning system rather than a backdrop, which gives the script real story-generating texture.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is controlled, unnerving, and quietly satirical, with a clean visual language that makes the institutional spaces feel emotionally radioactive. The final turn into public-facing propaganda gives the piece a distinct, chilling aftertaste.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real seeds of deeper thematic material here around consent, social engineering, and the monetization of intimacy. The script mostly plays the surface cleanly, but the Chance/Union machinery suggests a larger ideological system beneath the romance.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Lewis/Emma is the core engine, and Lewis/Darren/Dana/Chance each add a different pressure vector, but this is not a relationship-dense ensemble piece. The supporting characters are effective as forces, less so as recurring material generators.

lead_characters.name: Lewis
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, working-class, likely white; a young adult apprentice inside the Union system.
lead_characters.hook: Lewis is a hyper-compliant young man whose body language, speech, and choices have been trained into obedience, but whose emotional life keeps breaking the surface. He starts as a model participant in the Union’s pairing culture and becomes the one person willing to risk status, access, and safety for something that feels unscripted.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young Adam Driver or Timothée Chalamet performance in a controlled-pressure role: the actor gets to play repression, micro-rebellion, and a slow moral awakening all in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Emma
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, local to Northern California; Union participant with a more instinctive, less rigid relationship to the system.
lead_characters.hook: Emma is the script’s destabilizer: observant, lightly subversive, and emotionally clearer than the world around her. She’s not a manic rebel; she’s someone who can see the machinery and still choose intimacy, which makes her feel both grounded and dangerous to the system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the cool, self-possessed edge of Jodie Comer in The Last Duel or Daisy Edgar-Jones in Normal People: chemistry, intelligence, and the ability to make restraint feel alive.

lead_characters.name: Chance Hunter
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, public-facing leader of the Union; polished, charismatic, politically powerful.
lead_characters.hook: Chance is the smiling face of coercion, a man who can sound reasonable while tightening the screws. He’s not a cartoon villain; he’s the kind of institutional operator who understands that control works best when it feels like care.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is premium antagonist material in the vein of Michael Shannon in Boardwalk Empire or Matthew Macfadyen in Succession: a role built on charm, menace, and the pleasure of watching a smart actor weaponize calm.

lead_characters.name: Darren
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, Lewis’s father; working-class, structure-oriented, emotionally guarded.
lead_characters.hook: Darren is the father who believes discipline is love because it’s the only language he trusts. He’s not written as a monster; he’s the domestic face of the system, which makes him more painful than a simple antagonist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a veteran character actor do the John Goodman-in-10 Cloverfield Lane thing: warmth, authority, and a slow reveal of how ideology lives inside family life.

lead_characters.name: Dana
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 50s, Lewis’s mother; emotionally perceptive, quietly dissenting, domestic caretaker.
lead_characters.hook: Dana is the script’s most humanizing parental presence, the one who can hear the difference between compliance and truth. She’s gentle but not passive, and her scenes give the movie its clearest sense of what gets lost when people outsource intimacy to a system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting-mother territory in the Annette Bening / Laura Linney lane: a role that rewards stillness, subtext, and the ability to make one kitchen conversation carry the movie’s moral center.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, Union participant and campaign-side worker.
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is the polished version of the system’s logic: articulate, measured, and emotionally disciplined. She’s important because she shows Lewis what the Union produces when it works exactly as designed.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp supporting role for an actor who can play intelligence without warmth, in the mode of Sarah Snook’s precision work or Carrie Coon’s controlled social authority.

lead_characters.name: Lila
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, Emma’s friend; local, loose, unfiltered.
lead_characters.hook: Lila functions as Emma’s outside voice, the person who can say what the system won’t allow anyone else to say out loud. She’s a useful pressure valve and gives the coastal material a lived-in, less institutional texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing supporting part that lets an actor do fast, naturalistic banter and make a small role feel like a real person, similar to the best friend roles in indie relationship dramas.

lead_characters.name: Waitress
lead_characters.demographics: Female, adult, service worker in a Union-approved space.
lead_characters.hook: The waitress is a small but telling embodiment of how the system sorts people instantly by status and affiliation. Her reaction to Lewis’s Union ID is one of the script’s cleanest social tells.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, behavior-driven role that gives an actor a sharp reaction beat and a chance to define a whole social world in a few lines.

lead_characters.name: Receptionist
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 50s, administrative worker in the Union bureaucracy.
lead_characters.hook: The receptionist is the face of procedural indifference until Lewis’s request crosses into executive review and she has to reveal the system’s hidden hierarchy. She’s a great example of how the script turns ordinary bureaucracy into suspense.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong utility role for a seasoned character actor who can shift from neutral procedure to quiet alarm without changing the temperature of the room.

casting_characteristics: Lead is a young adult male with a highly controlled, internal performance style
Chance Hunter needs strong charisma and institutional authority
Emma requires chemistry and a naturalistic, unforced presence
Parents are age-specific 50s roles with emotional nuance

notable_requirements: Washington State, Oregon, and Northern California settings
Modern institutional interiors, approved restaurants, compound residence, coastal exteriors

technical.vfx_details: Mostly interface graphics, signage, broadcast overlays, and a few controlled screen inserts; no major creature or environment work.
technical.sfx_needs: One gunshot death at the gas station, convoy movement, and practical blood effects.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a streamer-led prestige genre release or specialty theatrical with awards-adjacent positioning.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the multi-state road travel, convoy logistics, border checkpoint, compound exteriors, and night work will keep this above a simple single-city indie.

casting.note: Lewis and Chance are the key lifts: Lewis needs a very specific internalized lead performance, and Chance needs enough charisma to make coercion feel seductive rather than cartoonish.

development.note: The final propaganda turn is the script’s defining move, but it also means the buyer has to be comfortable with a story that ends as a political-satirical reveal rather than a conventional romantic payoff.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated dystopian thrillers with a romantic engine and a political edge.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-54, slightly female-leaning, educated urban/suburban audience, strong streamer audience with appetite for prestige genre.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, modest VFX, limited action, and a cast built around one strong lead and a few key supporting roles keep this in indie feature territory.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building adult genre
director-driven buyers looking for a contained high-concept feature
actor-led packages seeking awards-adjacent genre material
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where social allegory, romance, and institutional paranoia can coexist without needing tentpole scale. The script is built for buyers who want a clean hook, a strong lead role, and a world that can be sold in one image.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the core engine is Lewis’s one-off collision with the Union system, and there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector on the page.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The dating system is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives buyers a clean, high-concept hook that can be marketed in a single sentence and a single image. That makes it unusually easy to position for streamer discovery and trailer-first selling.
strengths.evidence: The Union app, outing scores, cross-local restrictions, and the timed restaurant dates all make romance feel like a regulated civic process.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Lewis is a strong internal lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of part that can elevate a young actor and give the project a real performance anchor. Buyers can package around a breakout or a prestige name because the role is built on micro-shifts, not just plot mechanics.
strengths.evidence: His repeated self-corrections, posture adjustments, and the way he almost tells the truth before stopping himself.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels operational, not decorative.
strengths.what_it_means: The Union has enough rules, signage, and procedural language to support a full feature without feeling thin. That makes the movie feel more expensive and more complete than a simple allegory.
strengths.evidence: Approved restaurants, behavioral review, executive consultation, cross-local clearance, and the convoy border escort.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Chance Hunter is a premium antagonist.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has a buyer-friendly villain who can be played as charismatic rather than monstrous, which broadens casting and sharpens the marketing promise. That’s valuable for both prestige buyers and genre buyers.
strengths.evidence: His warm handshake, ranch anecdotes, and the way he turns Lewis’s sincerity into a controlled asset.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending reframes the whole movie.
strengths.what_it_means: The propaganda montage turns the romance into a political product, which gives the film a memorable final impression and a sharper thematic aftertaste. That kind of ending can lift a project from merely clever to conversation-worthy.
strengths.evidence: The interview, the broadcast package, the wedding imagery, and the final stable session reveal.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept prestige thriller with a breakout lead role and a world that sells itself fast. The romance engine is emotionally legible, the institutional machinery is specific enough to feel expensive, and the ending gives the movie a sharp satirical sting that should travel well with streamer and specialty buyers alike.

items.area: The final propaganda turn narrows the payoff.
items.detail: The ending deliberately converts the romance into a public-facing Union asset, which is thematically smart but also means the movie lands less as a cathartic love story than as a controlled ideological reveal. That’s a strong artistic choice, but it will be a conversation point for buyers expecting a more emotionally resolving finish.

A meaningful stretch of the script lives in dates, reports, approvals, and bureaucratic escalation, which clarifies the world but also keeps the engine in a measured register. The buyer conversation here is whether that controlled pace reads as tension or as a deliberate cool-down between bigger turns.

items.area: The supporting cast is more functional than deep.
items.detail: Darren, Dana, Shannon, Lila, the receptionist, and the waitress all do useful work, but most of them operate as pressure vectors rather than fully independent story engines. That keeps the script focused, but it also limits ensemble value and reduces the number of roles that can be used as packaging leverage.

items.area: The gas-station death is a hard tonal pivot.
items.detail: The owner’s shooting is the script’s most abrupt violence beat, and it shifts the movie from controlled dystopian romance into overt state brutality in one scene. That’s effective as escalation, but it’s also the moment most likely to define the content conversation for buyers and audiences.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest strength is also its biggest buyer conversation: it starts as a controlled romance and ends as a propaganda machine, which is smart but less emotionally conventional than a straight love-story payoff. The other friction is structural rather than conceptual — the middle is intentionally procedural, and the supporting cast is effective without being especially packaging-rich.
